name: Newfoundland and Labrador
summary_text: Newfoundland and Labrador stands under the Canadian federal framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017, and courts have applied those protections consistently. No Canadian jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities. Entry carries no trans-specific friction: Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers, and federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker. Provincial healthcare coverage is universal.  Legal gender recognition in the province operates without a surgery requirement. An amendment to the Vital Statistics Act, 2009, given Royal Assent 13 April 2016, removed the requirement to undergo sex-reassignment surgery before changing the gender marker on a birth or marriage registration, bringing provincial law into compliance with a December 2015 ruling of a Board of Inquiry under the provincial Human Rights Commission on complaints brought by two trans women.  A second amendment, given Royal Assent 23 June 2021, extended the route to residents who were not born in the province but have lived there at least three months. The change certificate costs $25, counts as official provincial identification, and can be used to update records in other jurisdictions; it serves as the identification document for people born outside Canada. The same amendment aligned with earlier changes allowing a non-binary option on provincial birth certificates.  Current requirements on the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador's official page: applicants must be 16 or older, or be represented by a parent or legal guardian for under-16s, with consent of the other parent or guardian and written consent of individuals aged 12 to 15. Applicants must be born in the province or have resided there at least three months. There is no fee for the change application itself; charges apply only to official copies of updated documents ($35 for a new birth certificate, $30 online).  One documented cross-border caveat applies. The province states it cannot guarantee that a birth certificate carrying an X gender marker will be accepted by authorities in other organisations, so a provincial record with that marker may not travel cleanly.  Police-reported hate-crime data is favourable for the province but rests on small numbers. Statistics Canada (30 March 2026 release, 2024 data) recorded 4,882 hate-crime incidents nationally, up 1% on 2023 after a 34% jump the previous year, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. Newfoundland and Labrador had the joint-lowest provincial rate at 5.3 per 100,000, tied with Manitoba, against Ontario's highest at 16.0. The province's recorded rise of 51% reflects 19 incidents in 2023 against 29 in 2024, so the percentage change is statistically fragile. Police figures capture only reported incidents. Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report examines national police-reported data including offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity; Egale Canada is an LGBTIQ+ organisation.

name: Nova Scotia
summary_text: Nova Scotia stands under the national framework of Canada. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017, and courts have applied those protections consistently. No jurisdiction in Canada restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply uniformly in Nova Scotia.  Legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration. Most provinces allow the gender marker on official documents to be changed by declaring one's identified gender; Prince Edward Island's 2016 amendment to its Vital Statistics Act removed the prior surgery requirement and replaced it with a declaration supported by a doctor's letter. Federally, identity documents can carry an X marker. Entry into Canada carries no trans-specific friction.  Correctional placement is the weakest point in the Nova Scotia record. The Chronicle Herald reported on 18 March 2025 that a federal judge gave a transgender woman from the Halifax region more time to file her application for judicial review of the decision to hold her in a men's prison while she serves a two-year robbery sentence. The judge cited a lack of transparency and clear, timely communication in the institutional decision-making, and systemic barriers that restricted the applicant's access to her lawyer. Federal policy after Bill C-16 is that transgender prisoners are to be placed according to their gender identity, so the case turns on whether that policy is being applied in the province's custodial system.  Nova Scotia's provincial government operates an explicit inclusion framework rather than restrictive trans-specific legislation. On 8 January 2026 it released the province's first 2SLGBTQIA+ Action Plan, developed under the Dismantling Racism and Hate Act passed in 2022, described as the first Canadian law of its kind to explicitly acknowledge 2SLGBTQIA+ people, and informed by more than 600 community members through surveys, virtual meetings and consultations. On 10 June 2026 the province announced more than $176,000 through the first round of its 2SLGBTQIA+ Community Impact Grant program.  National hate-crime data does not resolve trans-specific risk in the province. Statistics Canada reported on 30 March 2026 that 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents were recorded nationally in 2024, 1% above 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000, down 2% in 2024 and up 142% since 2018, with eight provinces recording stable or declining rates. The release carries no Nova Scotia-specific rate or incident count, and it breaks out sexual orientation as a motivation category rather than gender identity, so trans-specific hate-crime volume is not established by this dataset.
